nodes.summary: Bandit Level 0 — log in to a remote Linux server over SSH on port 2220, the skill every other OverTheWire level builds on.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 0

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 1 — find and read a file named readme in your home directory using ls and cat.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 1

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 10 — extract readable text from a binary file with strings and filter it with grep.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 10

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 11 — decode Base64 data, learning that encoding is not encryption.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 11

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 12 — undo a ROT13 substitution cipher with the tr command.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 12

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 13 — peel back layers of a hexdump, gzip, bzip2 and tar by repeatedly identifying and unpacking the file.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 13

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 14 — authenticate to SSH with a private key instead of a password.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 14

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 15 — talk to a plain-text network service on localhost with netcat.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 15

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 16 — talk to a TLS-encrypted service on localhost using openssl sclient.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 16

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 17 — scan a range of ports with nmap, tell TLS from plain services, and find the one that returns credentials.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 17

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 18 — compare two files with diff to find the single line that changed.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 18

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 19 — read a file even though .bashrc logs you out, by running a command remotely instead of opening a shell.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 19

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 2 — read a file literally named "-" and learn why commands treat a leading dash as an option.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 2

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 20 — use a setuid binary to read a file owned by another user, and learn what the setuid permission bit means.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 20

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 21 — run your own network listener in the background so a setuid program can connect to it.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 21

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 22 — read a cron job's configuration and script to see what a scheduled task does.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 22

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 23 — read a shell script run by cron and work out what it computes and for whom.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 23

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 24 — write your first shell script and let a cron job run it with more privileges than you have.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 24

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 25 — brute-force a 4-digit PIN against a network service by scripting 10,000 guesses over one connection.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 25

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 26 — discover that a user's login shell is not bash, then break out of the restricted program that replaced it.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 26

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 27 — you already have a shell as bandit26; use a setuid helper in its home directory to read the next password.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 27

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 28 — clone a Git repository over SSH from your own machine and read its files.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 28

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 29 — find a secret that was removed from the current files but is still preserved in Git history.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 29

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 3 — read a file whose name contains spaces by using quoting, escaping or tab completion.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 3

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 30 — discover that the interesting commit lives on a branch other than the one you cloned.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 30

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 31 — find a secret stored in a Git tag rather than in any file or branch.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 31

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 32 — push a commit to a Git remote and defeat a .gitignore rule that stops your file from being added.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 32

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 33 — escape from a shell that converts everything you type to uppercase.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 33

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 34 — a placeholder page: this level does not exist yet, so Level 33 is where Bandit currently ends.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 34

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 4 — find a hidden dotfile inside the inhere directory with ls -a.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 4

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 5 — identify the one human-readable file among many using the file command.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 5

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 6 — use find to locate a file by size and permissions in a directory tree.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 6

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 7 — search the whole server with find for a file owned by a given user and group, and silence permission errors.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 7

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 8 — find one line in a large text file with grep.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 8

nodes.summary: Bandit Level 9 — find the only unique line in a file by pairing sort with uniq through a pipe.
nodes.title: Bandit Level 9

nodes.summary: Bandit is the beginner Linux and SSH wargame — 34 short levels that teach the command-line skills every other OverTheWire game assumes.
nodes.title: Bandit

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 0 — a program that asks for a password; learn to find what it compares your input to by tracing and string extraction.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 0

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 1 — a classic stack buffer overflow in a binary without source, where you inject shellcode and redirect execution to it.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 1

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 2 — a privileged program runs another program by name, so how it finds that program becomes the weakness.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 2

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 3 — a format-string vulnerability in a binary without source, used to write to memory and take control.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 3

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 4 — a program reads a file whose name depends on its process ID, which opens the door to a race condition using symbolic links.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 4

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 5 — a privileged program sends data over the network to localhost, so you must set up a listener to receive it.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 5

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 6 — a later level that combines custom shellcode with a helper program; investigate the level directory and the program's behaviour.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 6

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 7 — one of the last Behemoth levels, where you apply everything learned so far to a binary that gives no hints.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 7

nodes.summary: Behemoth Level 8 — the last Behemoth page in this mirror; use it to consolidate your skills and decide what to study next.
nodes.title: Behemoth Level 8

nodes.summary: Behemoth is an intermediate wargame of 9 levels on buffer overflows, format strings and race conditions in binaries given without source.
nodes.title: Behemoth

nodes.summary: Blacksun Level 0 — exploit a remote format-string bug in a binary with ASLR, PIE and stack protection by using direct parameter access to study the stack.
nodes.title: Blacksun Level 0

nodes.summary: Blacksun Level 1 — a trivial stack overflow in a binary with ASLR but no PIE and no stack protector, so fixed program addresses can be used.
nodes.title: Blacksun Level 1

nodes.summary: Blacksun Level 2 — write a malicious POP3 server that triggers a vulnerability in a buggy mail-client library and gets a shell despite ASLR.
nodes.title: Blacksun Level 2

nodes.summary: Blacksun Level 3 — analyse a stripped binary with little documentation, work out what it expects, and exploit it, with some brute force.
nodes.title: Blacksun Level 3

nodes.summary: Blacksun Level 4 — exploit a deliberately introduced heap vulnerability in Apache and PHP by running your own PHP code on the server.
nodes.title: Blacksun Level 4

nodes.summary: Blacksun is an advanced exploitation wargame (currently down) about attacking hardened hosts that use ASLR, non-executable memory and stack protection.
nodes.title: Blacksun

nodes.summary: Blacksun reading list — papers on format strings, heap exploitation, frame-pointer overwrites, ASLR, PaX, stack protection and hardware defences.
nodes.title: Blacksun reading material

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 0 — talk to an encrypted remote system-call proxy that you must drive with correctly formed syscalls to read a password file.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 0

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 1 — a file-parsing heap corruption bug in C++ code, where overwriting an object's virtual-function pointer redirects execution.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 1

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 10 — additional practice with a non-executable stack, relying on careful reverse engineering.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 10

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 11 — the executable base and the stack are randomised, so you must defeat ASLR to get code execution.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 11

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 12 — a remote-procedure-call style reverse-engineering challenge.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 12

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 13 — "challenge your preconceptions of what's possible": an open-ended level with no description of the technique.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 13

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 14 — a vulnerability in a third-party library, with extra code present that may make exploiting it easier.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 14

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 15 — "Explosive decompression": a level hinting at a decompression-related weakness.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 15

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 2 — a simple stack overflow whose side effects get in the way of debugging and of launching a program directly with execve.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 2

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 3 — a remote heap corruption bug in a program linked against an old malloc implementation, with source supplied.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 3

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 4 — a binary that needs simple analysis, with a hint to keep resource limits in mind.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 4

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 5 — a series of logic and mathematics games, one of which is always solvable and can be understood by reverse engineering.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 5

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 6 — a simple remote daemon with a format-string vulnerability, left in a deliberately vulnerable state.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 6

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 7 — "Gentleman, start your disassemblers": a reverse-engineering level with IDA recommended.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 7

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 8 — a Phrack Search Daemon runs on the server without its GPLv2 source available, so bug hunting and custom shellcode may be needed.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 8

nodes.summary: Drifter Level 9 — escalate privileges by working out a secret file format and exploiting security oversights.
nodes.title: Drifter Level 9

nodes.summary: Drifter is a 16-level advanced wargame in the style of Vortex, mixing remote services, heap bugs, format strings, reversing and ASLR bypass.
nodes.title: Drifter

nodes.summary: Krypton Level 2 — break a Caesar cipher by feeding the provided encryption program known text and watching how it responds.

nodes.summary: Krypton Level 3 — recover a substitution key from several intercepted English messages using frequency analysis.

nodes.summary: Krypton Level 4 — break a Vigenère cipher when you know the key length, by treating each position as a separate Caesar problem.

nodes.summary: Krypton Level 6 — move from classical ciphers to stream ciphers and exploit a weak pseudo-random keystream using a known-plaintext attack.

nodes.summary: Leviathan Level 3 — another password-checking program; apply what you learned about tracing and compare with the earlier level.

nodes.summary: Leviathan Level 4 — find a program whose output is a string of binary digits and learn to convert numbers between bases.

nodes.summary: Leviathan Level 5 — a setuid program reads a file from a fixed path; learn how symbolic links redirect it.

nodes.summary: Leviathan Level 6 — a program wants a four-digit code; learn to brute-force a small secret with a shell loop.

nodes.summary: Narnia is the first binary-exploitation wargame — 10 levels where you read C source code and abuse common memory bugs like overflows and format strings.
nodes.title: Narnia

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 0 — overflow a buffer to overwrite a neighbouring variable and learn how data is laid out in memory.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 0

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 1 — the program runs code taken from an environment variable; learn what shellcode is and how to supply it.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 1

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 2 — a classic stack buffer overflow where you overwrite the saved return address to take control of execution.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 2

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 3 — another overflow level; use the source to see what an overflowing input can reach and plan around the program's file handling.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 3

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 4 — a stack overflow where the environment has been cleared, so your injected code must live in the buffer itself.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 4

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 5 — a format-string bug; learn how printf-style functions can be made to read and write arbitrary memory.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 5

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 6 — a harder overflow where relying on injected shellcode is unattractive; think about reusing code that already exists in the program.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 6

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 7 — a format-string bug again, this time used to redirect a function pointer.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 7

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 8 — a later Narnia level that combines the earlier techniques; use the source and a debugger to find where your input goes.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 8

nodes.summary: Narnia Level 9 — the final Narnia page in this mirror; apply everything from Levels 0–8 and consolidate your exploitation skills.
nodes.title: Narnia Level 9

nodes.summary: Natas teaches server-side web security through 35 browser-based levels, from reading page source to SQL injection, session attacks and cryptographic oracles.
nodes.title: Natas

nodes.summary: Natas Level 0 — sign in to the first website and find a password the page does not show you but still sends to your browser.
nodes.title: Natas Level 0

nodes.summary: Natas Level 1 — the same secret is hidden in the page, but the site tries to stop you viewing it; learn why client-side restrictions are not security.
nodes.title: Natas Level 1

nodes.summary: Natas Level 10 — the site now filters dangerous characters; learn why blocklists fail and how a legitimate tool's own features can be bent to your purpose.
nodes.title: Natas Level 10

nodes.summary: Natas Level 11 — a cookie is "encrypted" with repeating-key XOR; learn how a known plaintext reveals the key and lets you forge the cookie.
nodes.title: Natas Level 11

nodes.summary: Natas Level 12 — upload a file the server stores and then serves; learn why trusting the client's filename and file type lets attackers run their own code.
nodes.title: Natas Level 12

nodes.summary: Natas Level 13 — the server now checks that an upload looks like an image; learn what file signatures are and why checking them is not enough.
nodes.title: Natas Level 13

nodes.summary: Natas Level 14 — a login form builds its SQL query by pasting in your input; learn the basics of SQL injection and authentication bypass.
nodes.title: Natas Level 14

nodes.summary: Natas Level 15 — the application only answers "exists" or "does not exist"; learn blind boolean SQL injection and how to automate it.
nodes.title: Natas Level 15

nodes.summary: Natas Level 16 — command injection returns, but with stricter filtering and no visible output; learn to turn a search tool into a yes/no oracle.
nodes.title: Natas Level 16

nodes.summary: Natas Level 17 — the application gives no feedback at all; learn time-based blind SQL injection, where a deliberate delay is the answer.
nodes.title: Natas Level 17

nodes.summary: Natas Level 18 — session identifiers come from a small number space; learn how predictable session IDs can be brute-forced to hijack an admin session.
nodes.title: Natas Level 18

nodes.summary: Natas Level 19 — session IDs look random but encode the username; learn to see structure in what appears to be gibberish.
nodes.title: Natas Level 19

nodes.summary: Natas Level 2 — notice that the page loads a resource you can follow, and discover what an exposed directory listing reveals.
nodes.title: Natas Level 2

nodes.summary: Natas Level 20 — a custom session file handler trusts a newline in user input; learn how data written to server-side state can be forged.
nodes.title: Natas Level 20

nodes.summary: Natas Level 21 — two related sites share one session store; learn how an application you can influence can poison a more trusted one.
nodes.title: Natas Level 21

nodes.summary: Natas Level 22 — the server redirects you away, but still sends the page body; learn that a redirect does not stop the content from being delivered.
nodes.title: Natas Level 22

nodes.summary: Natas Level 23 — a password check mixes string search with a numeric comparison; learn how PHP's loose typing can be satisfied in surprising ways.
nodes.title: Natas Level 23

nodes.summary: Natas Level 24 — a password check uses strcmp, which behaves unexpectedly when it is given the wrong type of input; learn PHP type confusion.
nodes.title: Natas Level 24

nodes.summary: Natas Level 25 — a weak path filter and a logged User-Agent combine into log poisoning; learn how reading a log file can execute attacker-supplied code.
nodes.title: Natas Level 25

nodes.summary: Natas Level 26 — a cookie contains serialised PHP data the server later unserialises; learn how object injection can write files on the server.
nodes.title: Natas Level 26

nodes.summary: Natas Level 27 — a registration and login system that compares trimmed values; learn how database column truncation can create a duplicate account.
nodes.title: Natas Level 27

nodes.summary: Natas Level 28 — a query is encrypted with AES in ECB mode; learn how block-by-block encryption lets an attacker cut and paste ciphertext.
nodes.title: Natas Level 28

nodes.summary: Natas Level 29 — a Perl script opens a filename taken from the request; learn how Perl's open function can run commands.
nodes.title: Natas Level 29

nodes.summary: Natas Level 3 — learn how robots.txt, meant to guide search engines, can instead point an attacker at the very paths you wanted hidden.
nodes.title: Natas Level 3

nodes.summary: Natas Level 30 — a Perl database call quotes a single value, but not when it receives a list; learn how SQL injection survives an escaping function.
nodes.title: Natas Level 30

nodes.summary: Natas Level 31 — a CSV upload feature passes a file handle to Perl's diamond operator; learn how that can read arbitrary files.
nodes.title: Natas Level 31

nodes.summary: Natas Level 32 — the same Perl file-reading trick is back, but now the goal is running a command; learn how to turn a file read into execution.
nodes.title: Natas Level 32

nodes.summary: Natas Level 33 — an upload checker and a file function combine so that a crafted archive triggers deserialisation; learn about PHP phar attacks.
nodes.title: Natas Level 33

nodes.summary: Natas Level 34 — the final published Natas level; there is no further password, so use it to consolidate what you have learned.
nodes.title: Natas Level 34

nodes.summary: Natas Level 4 — the server decides who you are from the Referer header, which you control; learn to craft and modify HTTP requests.
nodes.title: Natas Level 4

nodes.summary: Natas Level 5 — a login state is stored in a cookie the user can edit; learn to inspect and change cookies.
nodes.title: Natas Level 5

nodes.summary: Natas Level 6 — read the server-side logic the site exposes and follow it to a file that holds the secret, learning how sensitive includes leak.
nodes.title: Natas Level 6

nodes.summary: Natas Level 7 — a page parameter chooses which file is shown; learn about path traversal and local file inclusion.
nodes.title: Natas Level 7

nodes.summary: Natas Level 8 — reverse a chain of encodings found in the source to work out the secret, and learn that obfuscation is not encryption.
nodes.title: Natas Level 8

nodes.summary: Natas Level 9 — user input is passed into a shell command; learn what OS command injection is and why shell metacharacters are dangerous.
nodes.title: Natas Level 9

nodes.summary: Semtex is an older (currently offline) wargame of 13 levels on network programming, reverse engineering, buffer overflows and combinatorial analysis.
nodes.title: Semtex

nodes.summary: Semtex Level 0 — receive a stream from a network port, discard every second byte, and run the executable that reveals the password.
nodes.title: Semtex Level 0

nodes.summary: Semtex Level 1 — reverse engineer a simple encryption tool and decrypt a given ciphertext.
nodes.title: Semtex Level 1

nodes.summary: Semtex Level 10 — exploit a weakness in how an authentication daemon checks passwords, in the style of old Windows 95/98 network shares.
nodes.title: Semtex Level 10

nodes.summary: Semtex Level 11 — "Déjà vu": a modified version of an earlier encryption tool, with process plumbing (popen, dup2) suggested as reading.
nodes.title: Semtex Level 11
